video_title: What the US-Japan Currency Intervention Means for the Yen, Rates, and the Dollar
gist: Goldman's Karen Fishman (FX Research) and Praneet Shah (FX options trading) dissect Japan's July 30, 2026 intervention - an estimated $85bn+ MOF dollar-selling operation joined by a token ~$1-2bn US leg - and argue the US participation was about Treasury-market functioning, not a view on where the yen should trade. Both conclude intervention only buys time: dollar/yen has already retraced from a 5% high-to-low move to 3% net, making the September BOJ decision (65% priced for 25bp) and US CPI the real variables, while Praneet flags a 25% undervalued yen and a 100bp hedged JGB yield pickup as the seeds of a multi-year structural reversal.

insights.claim: Japan sold US dollars to buy yen starting July 30, 2026 in an estimated up-to-$85bn operation across July 30-31, with possibly more on August 3 - the largest FX intervention in 15 years and Japan's biggest two-day intervention on record outside October 2011, after the yen hit 40-year lows versus the dollar.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Sets the scale benchmark for any repeat operation; official MOF numbers land about a month later and could confirm or undercut the $85bn estimate.
insights.quote: probably amounted to up to $85 billion

insights.claim: The trading-desk breakdown was roughly $60bn on the Thursday, $25bn on the Friday and possibly another $20bn on the Monday against about $30bn of average daily dollar/yen volume, while EBS - the main spot venue, normally $5-10bn a day - printed roughly $90bn Thursday and $80bn Friday.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: EBS volume running roughly 10x normal is a real-time, publicly observable tell that intervention is underway well before any official confirmation.

insights.claim: The operation deliberately broke every heuristic traders use to anticipate Japanese intervention: no forewarning unlike April/May, realized volatility was not elevated, dollar/yen at 164 had already traded there earlier that month, the Bank of Japan was due to set rates the next day, and the $60bn Thursday tranche was executed in a very short window rather than spread out.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: The old predictors of MOF action are now unreliable, so short-yen carry positions must be sized for ambush risk at any level and on any day.
insights.quote: these are all conditions that had set the scene such that traders on the seat didn't really expect this to happen

themes.theme: Why the US Joined: Market Functioning, Not the Yen Level

insights.claim: Goldman FX research believes US participation in the July intervention was primarily about limiting volatility in US markets rather than endorsing a level for the yen, and explicitly frames it as a signal of support rather than a directional view on the currency.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Do not read coordination as a US commitment to a stronger yen; the US reaction function is Treasury-market stress, so watch US rates volatility rather than dollar/yen to predict the next assist.
insights.quote: it does seem to really be more about the signal of support and ultimately the US' focus on market conditions rather than taking a strong view on where the yen should be

insights.claim: The US administration has been encouraging expansion and use of the Fed facility that lets foreign central banks raise dollar cash by selling Treasuries to the Fed under agreement to buy them back, which lets Japan fund intervention without dumping Treasuries on the secondary market and pushing US yields abruptly higher.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Breaks the historical link between Japanese intervention and upward pressure on US yields, and is the clearest evidence that US policy here is defending Treasury market functioning.

insights.claim: US involvement tracks US rates volatility rather than yen weakness: in January both sides signalled intervention but did not act, in April Japan acted alone, and in July the US joined - and both January and July featured elevated US interest-rate volatility going in while April did not.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: A reusable predictor: rising US rates vol raises the odds of another coordinated operation, while pure yen weakness only implies a unilateral Japanese one.

insights.claim: The US leg of coordinated interventions has historically been only about $1-2bn, making it a signalling instrument rather than a flow-driving one.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: The US contribution is nearly costless, so coordination carries far less policy commitment than its market impact implies - a fragile foundation for a sustained yen rally.
insights.quote: It's been historically around one to two billion dollars. So again, more about the signal than actually driving the currency in a certain direction.

insights.claim: The token US leg moved dollar/yen a further 2% on top of Japan's 3% move despite trading a tiny fraction of the MOF's volume, showing the symbolism of coordination is worth more than the flow behind it.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Coordination headlines, not intervention size, are the high-convexity event to hedge around.
insights.quote: they managed to move it 2% despite significantly less volumes compared to the $85 billion that the MOF

themes.theme: Positioning Unwind and the Euro/Yen Flank

insights.claim: CFTC data released the day of the recording showed the fourth largest absolute reduction in yen positioning in 20 years of history, quantifying how much speculative squaring the intervention forced.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Much of the short-yen overhang has already been flushed, reducing the fuel available for another intervention-driven squeeze.
insights.quote: It's actually the fourth largest absolute reduction in yen positioning in the 20-year history that you've seen

insights.claim: A 3% single-day drop in dollar/yen wipes out the entire 2%-2.5% annualized carry that is the main reason to be long the pair, which mechanically forces levered hedge funds and CTAs to stop out.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: The carry cushion in yen shorts is now so thin that one intervention day destroys a year of return - the risk/reward is far worse than the yield suggests.
insights.quote: if dollar/yen just suddenly gaps 3% lower in a given day, that's your entire annualized carry just wiped out in one move

insights.claim: Breaking below 158 in dollar/yen, the 200-day moving average, was the key technical catalyst that turned the intervention into a broad position-cutting event on the Thursday and Friday.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: 158 is the level to watch on any retest; a decisive break would likely trigger a second round of systematic liquidation.

insights.claim: Goldman's desk identifies 187.50 in euro/yen rather than any dollar/yen level as the apparent intervention trigger - it preceded both the April-May operation and July 30 - and client interest in expressing yen strength has consequently migrated from dollar/yen into the euro cross.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: A non-obvious tripwire: size short-yen risk off euro/yen 187.50, and note that crowding into that cross raises both payoff and unwind risk.
insights.quote: 187.50 to us looks like a key level in euro/yen. It triggered the April to May intervention back a few months ago.

insights.claim: Goldman's client flow after the intervention was unusually two-way: about half want continued yen strength targeting 150 in dollar/yen and a further 5% move in euro/yen, while the other half are buying the dip on the view that nothing structural has changed.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: No consensus after a record intervention means no positioning anchor - expect chop and extreme sensitivity to the September BOJ outcome.
insights.quote: half our client base want to play for continued yen strength, targeting a move even down to 150 in dollar/yen and a 5% move in euro/yen as well

insights.claim: Dollar/yen moved 5% from high to low during the intervention but has retraced to only 3% net - in line with past episodes despite far larger size - meaning Japan stabilized the exchange rate rather than reversing structural weakness and got materially less bang for buck.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Declining marginal efficacy argues the authorities must escalate to actual policy (rate hikes) rather than repeat the same operation.
insights.quote: they have had much less bang for buck

insights.claim: Intervention is not a sustainable fix and only buys time - it forces investors out of positions and mutes performance while they fear a repeat, but absent a subsequent policy shift the underlying currency pressures reemerge, exactly as after Japan's solo April-May operation, after which the yen hit 40-year lows within months.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: The historical base case is that intervention-driven yen strength decays within months, so fade rallies that are not confirmed by policy delivery.
insights.quote: So no, it's not a sustainable fix. It ultimately just buys some time.

insights.claim: Japan has ample capacity to intervene again - roughly $1 trillion of FX reserves in US dollars (Praneet cites $1.2 trillion) of which about $200bn is cash or cash equivalents, enough for another couple of rounds at near-record size, with the full trillion accessible in liquid form via the Fed's facility.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: A firepower-exhaustion thesis against Japan is unsupported; the binding constraint is willingness and policy, not reserves.

insights.claim: The signalling value of unlocking a trillion dollars of Japan's balance sheet via the Fed's FIMA facility - not the cash itself - was one of the main reasons clients turned bullish on the yen.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Any formal expansion or first Japanese use of the FIMA facility is a yen-bullish headline independent of actual dollar selling.
insights.quote: When you unlock a trillion dollars of the balance sheet that potentially now can be used for ready intervention, that's one of the main reasons that clients really did get quite bulled up on the yen

insights.claim: Two-week to one-month yen call options still carry significant risk premium, showing the market remains braced for another rapid gap lower in dollar/yen and euro/yen - a residual deterrent that works in the BOJ and MOF's favour without them spending anything.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Yen call premium is expensive but the authorities get free deterrence from it; selling those calls underwrites gap risk cheaply relative to the fresh precedent.
insights.quote: there's still significant risk premium in two-week to one-month yen call options

insights.claim: If dollar/yen trades back up into 160 the market will be reluctant to re-sell yen, because the priced drawdown risk from another intervention makes rebuilding shorts unattractive at that level.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: 160 becomes a soft ceiling on dollar/yen enforced by option-market deterrence rather than actual intervention - a level to fade rallies into.
insights.quote: If spot is trading up into 160, there's a real risk that you don't want to continue selling yen when you've got this large risk of a drawdown still priced by the market.

themes.theme: Carry Differential: BOJ Path and US Data

insights.claim: The overwhelming driver of dollar/yen is the carry differential, which splits into the path of Japanese rates and the path of US rates - making intervention a sideshow to those two variables.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Trade the yen off rate-differential catalysts (BOJ meetings, US CPI, payrolls) rather than intervention headlines, which only add noise around the trend.
insights.quote: the overwhelming driver of the exchange rate has really been the carry differential

insights.claim: Markets price a 65% chance of a 25bp Bank of Japan hike in September and 40bp of hikes into year-end; Praneet says the BOJ must deliver and hike faster than expected to address the medium-term drivers of yen weakness, and Karen states that failure to deliver in September would put renewed downward pressure on the yen.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah and Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs
insights.so_what: The September BOJ meeting is the single largest binary for the yen; a hold against 65% pricing triggers a sharp yen-negative repricing.
insights.quote: there's a 65% chance that they hike 25 basis points. That I think they really do need to deliver on

insights.claim: A soft US CPI print could relieve yen-weakness pressure and raise expectations of a follow-up intervention, following the July 2024 template where one of the most effective rounds of BOJ/MOF intervention landed on a US CPI miss and was reinforced by a subsequent payrolls miss.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Intervention efficacy is conditional on US data cooperating, so pair long-yen expressions with weak-US-data catalysts rather than trading them standalone.
insights.quote: You saw a miss in US CPI and one of the most effective rounds of BOJ MOF intervention was actually on that miss in US data

insights.claim: Yen weakness stems from Japan's domestic policy mix - large government spending plans plus only very gradual BOJ hikes - which markets read as inflationary, pushing real returns down and driving money offshore or into outright yen shorts.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: The fiscal-monetary mix, not FX policy, is the root cause; only fiscal restraint or faster hikes structurally fix the yen.
insights.quote: Markets view that combination as inflationary, so in other words, those rate hikes are insufficient to contain the rising inflation risk.

insights.claim: Despite volatility this year around AI, oil and Fed expectations, recession odds have not risen and FX volatility has stayed very low, removing safe-haven demand for the yen and creating an ideal carry-trade environment that compounded its weakness.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: A rise in recession odds or FX vol - an AI-driven growth scare, for instance - would do more for the yen than any intervention; Karen names AI worries explicitly as a potential trigger for sustained yen strength.

themes.theme: Structural Yen Case: Valuation vs Momentum

insights.claim: The yen has depreciated 45% over the last five years, an 8% compounded annual rate, which is the momentum reality a Japanese investor must be persuaded to trade against before repatriating capital.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Quantifies the hurdle rate for repatriation - domestic Japanese assets must beat an 8% annual currency tailwind on foreign holdings to attract flows home.
insights.quote: You've had 45% depreciation over the last five years, so that's an 8% compounded annual depreciation in the yen.

insights.claim: The yen starts 25% undervalued on a long-term valuation basis, and a Japanese investor now earns 100 basis points of extra yield on a 10-year JGB versus a currency-hedged 10-year US Treasury, alongside undervaluation in Japanese bonds and equities.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: For the first time in years the hedged carry math favours domestic JGBs over Treasuries for Japanese institutions - the mechanical precondition for repatriation flows is now in place.
insights.quote: for a Japanese investor on a 10-year JGB, you actually earn 100 basis points of extra yield when you compare that to a 10-year US Treasury currency hedged

insights.claim: Praneet argues that if policymakers get the decisions right and reverse the momentum of yen weakness, structural yen strengthening over the next few years is achievable given the valuation and hedged-yield setup - a more constructive medium-term view than current flows imply.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: A multi-year long-yen thesis exists that is independent of intervention and contingent only on BOJ delivery - the asymmetric setup for patient capital.
insights.quote: if you can reverse this momentum weaker in the yen, I do think there is something there where policymakers, if they get the decisions right, can reverse this trend and actually create some structural yen strengthening in the next few years

insights.claim: The Japanese administration has reportedly been focused on encouraging Japanese investors to shift back into domestic assets after a decade of raising their foreign-asset share at the expense of domestic holdings - a reversal Goldman says would be a meaningful source of sustained yen appreciation and part of why its models show the yen undervalued.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Repatriation policy is the highest-impact yen catalyst that is not priced; watch for concrete tax or regulatory incentives from Tokyo.

insights.claim: Karen tempers the repatriation thesis: such shifts take time and return prospects abroad remain more attractive than Japanese assets, so the flow reversal faces real hurdles even though it is the mechanism that would make yen strength sustained.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: A check on the constructive valuation case - the research and trading sides of Goldman differ on how quickly repatriation can realistically happen.
insights.quote: return prospects abroad are still more attractive than Japanese assets

themes.theme: Dollar Outlook and the Reserve-Currency Debate

insights.claim: The argument that helping a reserve manager sell Treasuries signals the US might later hinder such sales - eroding dollar reserve appeal - is a leap; Goldman argues the episode instead demonstrates that no other currency comes close to the dollar in usefulness, network effects and supporting infrastructure, while conceding unconventional policy choices can amplify institutional-reliability concerns as seen weighing on the dollar last year.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Pushes back on attaching a de-dollarization narrative to this intervention, while flagging that the institutional-credibility discount is dormant rather than dead.
insights.quote: no other currency currently comes close to the US dollar in terms of its usefulness, network effects, and the supporting infrastructure

insights.claim: Praneet argues the Fed facility's role in aiding market function actively supports the dollar's reserve-currency status and will not be a key determinant of the dollar's path; the Fed's reaction function and upcoming data matter far more going into the autumn.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: Trade the dollar off Fed pricing and inflation data, not institutional-credibility narratives.

insights.claim: Gold, CNH and the yen - the three pillars Praneet watches for the broad dollar - are all now starting to appreciate against the dollar, pointing to a steady glide weaker in the dollar driven by the inflation path and expected Fed reaction function into year-end rather than reserve-currency concerns.
insights.speaker: Praneet Shah, Goldman Sachs FX options trading
insights.so_what: A cross-asset confirmation framework: when gold, CNH and yen turn together, the broad dollar downtrend is the higher-probability path.
insights.quote: you've got gold, you've got CNH, you've got yen. All of them are now starting to appreciate against the dollar. So I do think we're going to now start to see a steady glide weaker in the dollar

insights.claim: Goldman Research's baseline of constructive risk sentiment, range-bound rate differentials, decent global growth and low FX volatility implies further modest dollar STRENGTH against low-yielders like the euro and yen and continued dollar weakness against higher-yielding EM currencies.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Research and the trading desk openly diverge - Karen's house view has dollar/yen grinding higher again while Praneet expects a broad dollar glide lower; the carry-versus-Fed axis is where that disagreement resolves.
insights.quote: we're projecting some further modest dollar strength against those low-yielding currencies like the euro and like the yen, but also some continued dollar weakness against those higher-yielding currencies, mainly in EM

insights.claim: A weaker, more volatile yen implies a stronger, more volatile dollar, which raises financial stability concerns and weighs on growth expectations in a self-amplifying loop - the spillover logic underpinning US interest in yen stability.
insights.speaker: Karen Fishman, Goldman Sachs Research
insights.so_what: Explains why the US keeps showing up: yen instability transmits into US financial conditions, so it is not treated as a foreign problem.
